A FOG—A PUBLIC EXECUTION.—From
A London letter to the New York Cour-
ier:


The densest fog known for years, over
hung London on Tuesday and Wednesday
nights. It was as thick as darkness, and
almost impenetrable. Gas lamps sent
forth mere flicker, and it was impossible
to see six feet distinctly. Men and boys
were selling "links," or flaming torches
and the greatest care was necessary in per-
ambulating the streets. It was dangerous

impossible, in so doing, to avoid being
knocked down by vehicles or horses. One
person at least, was killed, and several rob-
bed and lost. In the low lying parts of
the Metropolis, it was horrible, and all
were glad when it disappeared.


Among the events of the week was the
execution of a man in front of Newgate
prison. He was hung for murdering his
wife as an example of intimidation to bad
husbands. While he was on the scaffold,
a cadger picked man's packet almost un-
der the gallows, and that day three men
were arrested for beating their wives; two
of whom declared while flogging their con-
sorts, that they would yet kill them, and be
hung as was the man that morning at Old
Bailey. The scene was horrible, and at-
tended by about fifteen thousand of the
lowest characters in London, men, women
and children. Many of the men coolly
smoked their foul pipes while waiting to
see, and at the time of the execution.
